reason: auoit eſté commis is a finite clause after the full stop (iceluy Rapt auoit eſté commis … & par ainſi digne de mort, with eſtoit understood); the infinitive would hang awkwardly from conuaincu; the English is the same either way.
fi, = fin., the last paragraph of l. Qui coetu (D. 48.6.5.2, the one on carrying off a married woman); no paragraph of that law begins Si.
fœdiſsi-mam and fœdiſſi-mam are the same word, foedissimam (C. 9.9.20); only the form of the double s differs and the translation is unaffected.

The sacrilege canons, including c. Si quis contumax cited in the same note, stand in C. 17 q. 4, which note a cites as xvij. q. iiij.; q. iiij. keeps the questio consistent (the print's xvj. is itself probably a slip for xvij.). Translation unaffected.
The canon's incipit is Si quis contumax; the comma inside it in B is a stray sort. Translation unaffected.
Plutarque is the name; Plutarqne is a turned u.
The quotation continues (& apres vendu …), so the semicolon after freres suits the sentence; a full stop would cut it. Translation unaffected.
coniointe and conioincte are both sixteenth-century spellings of conjointe, 'joined'; translation unaffected.
ſi ꝗs and ſiqs both read si quis (ꝗs / qs the abbreviation of quis), the incipit of § Si quis volentem; translation unaffected.
Chapter 13 or 12 of book 3 of Crinito's De honesta disciplina; the work could not be checked here and the translation only reproduces the numeral (printed as xiij).
iu. abbreviates iudicum, the incipit of Novel 134 (Ut nulli iudicum); ius. is no part of the title.
l'intention is the word; ſ'intention is no word (a wrong sort for l'). Same line as p127-b0l0-2.
Same line as p127-b0l0-1, so the same choice; à and á (nuire à ſon prochain) translate the same.
c. = capitulum before the incipit Si quis propter necessitatem (X 5.18.3); e is a wrong sort.
pæ. is the abbreviation of pœnis (D. de poenis, as de pœn. in note d2); pa. is no recognisable abbreviation. Translation unaffected.
alleguee. ends the note; the hyphen of B would imply a continuation, and none follows (the next note begins l. lege.).
